lessonRef.unitTitle: PF6 — Protecting and Insuring: Naming Risk and Deciding What to Do About It
lessonRef.title: Transfer to a new case: accept, reduce, or transfer a risk

focus: accept, reduce, or transfer a risk
objective: Apply the accept, reduce, or transfer method to a new fictional risk where the answer differs from the earlier case, and say what changed to make it differ.
scenario: A fictional vehicle owner faces a simulated 8% annual chance of a $2,600 mechanical failure. The maintenance plan and the warranty below are invented for this exercise.
safetyNotes: Every figure, person, employer, institution, offer, account, and document on this task sheet is fictional and exists only for practice.
No real transaction is part of this lesson, and no real bank, card, brokerage, tax, or login detail is ever requested. If a task sheet ever appears to ask for one, stop and tell a trusted adult.
This lesson teaches general financial concepts and does not advise anyone about their own money. For a real decision, talk with a trusted adult or a qualified licensed professional.
materials: the three fictional options in these directions

tasks.directions: Accept: bear the $2,600 if it happens. Reduce: a $220 annual maintenance plan cuts the chance from 8% to 3%. Transfer: an extended warranty costs $180 a year and pays the repair less a $150 deductible.

prompts.text: What is the expected annual cost of accepting the risk?
What is the expected annual cost of reducing the risk?
What is the expected annual cost of transferring the risk?

tasks.directions: Compare with the earlier bicycle case, where accepting was cheapest at $93.00 against $100.00 to transfer.

prompts.text: Which option is cheapest here in expected annual cost?
choices: Transfer the risk with the warranty

prompts.text: What is the worst single-year cost of transferring here?
How much larger is the worst case of accepting than of transferring?
The same three-way method gave "accept" for the bicycle and "transfer" here. Name what changed between the two cases, and state the general rule the pair of cases supports.

remediation: If reducing looks cheapest, check the arithmetic on the maintenance plan: $220 is spent whether or not the failure happens, and it only removes five percentage points of an 8% chance. The certain spending outweighs what it buys.
extension: Find the maintenance price at which reducing would beat transferring, and say whether that price seems plausible for what it claims to do.
